results.title: Stumbling Into AI Emotional Dependence: How Routine AI Interactions Reshape Human Connection
results.summary: Public discourse and emerging policy typically assume that AI emotional support is a deliberate act: a lonely user consciously seeking comfort from a dedicated companion chatbot. In this paper, we draw on emerging empirical evidence and argue that this picture is inaccurate on two accounts, both in how AI emotional support arises and how it shapes future behavior. First, AI emotional support commonly emerges incidentally within task-oriented interactions on general-purpose platforms, much as workplace friendships deepen through collaboration. Second, these incidental encounters are path-dependent: positive experiences of AI emotional support update people's beliefs about AI's emotional capabilities and redirect their choices for future emotional support, increasing preference for AI and decreasing preference for humans. We review recent evidence, including a large-scale longitudinal study conducted in collaboration with OpenAI, showing that daily five-minute conversations with an AI about personal issues over 28 days led to a 10.3% decrease in the preference for seeking support from humans and an 11.6% increase in the preference for AI. These findings suggest that current policy, focused on companion apps and isolated interactions, cannot adequately protect human connection. Instead, effective regulations should extend to general-purpose AI systems and address cumulative, trajectory-level changes in how people seek support. Recognizing how people stumble into AI emotional support and how those encounters redirect human connections over time is essential to safeguarding human well-being.

results.title: Emotional Attachment: A Study on Emotional Design Strategies in Companion AI Products
results.summary: Abstract: With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, Companion AI products have reshaped the traditional human-computer interaction paradigm by virtue of sophisticated Emotional Design, forging in-depth emotional bonds with users and driving the evolution of human-machine relations toward complex intimate connections. However, the escalating anthropomorphism of AI has given rise to a prominent emotional dependence among a subset of users, which further triggers the paradox of "companionship-alienation": these products seemingly offer emotional consolation, yet in reality, they may exacerbate users' loneliness and erode their willingness and ability to engage in real-world social interactions. Against this backdrop, this study aims to systematically dissect this phenomenon and explore rational and sustainable emotional design strategies for companion AI products. This research adopts a case study approach as the core methodology, first clarifying the definition of Companion AI products — referring to AI robots or virtual dialogue agents with a certain level of intelligence, autonomy and social skills that can establish and maintain long-term relationships with users. Such products are capable of capturing both verbal content and non-verbal cues such as tone and emotion, and retain user preferences and personal historical information through memory functions to achieve personalized and coherent interaction. Based on functional characteristics and target user groups, the study categorizes current companion AI software products into four types: intelligent assistant type, role-playing dialogue partner type, AI social community type and emotional support tool type, each catering to users' instrumental needs, self-expression needs, social belonging needs and mental health needs respectively, forming a complementary product matrix. results.title: When companionship becomes dependence: Replika, emotional AI, and strategic boundaries in the AI companion economy
results.summary: This teaching case examines Replika, an AI companion platform developed by Luka Inc., and the strategic dilemma faced by founder and Chief Executive Officer Eugenia Kuyda in late 2025 as increasing regulatory and societal scrutiny challenged the company’s emotionally immersive engagement model. Replika differentiated itself through persistent one-to-one conversational relationships that fostered emotional continuity and drove subscription-based revenue growth. However, rising concerns regarding emotional dependency, prolonged engagement, and the substitution of human relationships by AI companions created mounting pressure for the company to reconsider the boundaries of its platform design. The case places Kuyda at a critical strategic crossroads: should Replika continue prioritizing deep emotional immersion as its primary competitive advantage, introduce clearer relational safeguards to align with emerging legitimacy expectations, or reposition the platform toward a less immersive form of AI-supported interaction? Situated within the rapidly evolving AI companion industry, the case provides rich material to explore platform governance, stakeholder legitimacy, business model dependence, strategic trade-offs, and long-term positioning under conditions of technological uncertainty and emerging regulation. The case is intended for postgraduate courses in strategic management, digital platform strategy, artificial intelligence governance, technology management, and executive education.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Digital Companion: Comfort and Emotional Engagement Among Youth in 2026
Negotiating Digital Identities with AI Companions: Motivations, Strategies, and Emotional Outcomes
results.summary: AI companions enable deep emotional relationships by engaging a user’s sense of identity, but they also pose risks like unhealthy emotional dependence. Mitigating these risks requires first understanding the underlying process of identity construction and negotiation with AI companions. Focusing on Character.AI (C.AI), a popular AI companion, we conducted an LLM-assisted thematic analysis of 22,374 online discussions on its subreddit. Using Identity Negotiation Theory as an analytical lens, we identified a three-stage process: 1) five user motivations; 2) an identity negotiation process involving three communication expectations and four identity co-construction strategies; and 3) three emotional outcomes. Our findings surface the identity work users perform as both performers and directors to co-construct identities in negotiation with C.AI. This process takes place within a socio-emotional sandbox where users can experiment with social roles and express emotions without non-human partners. Finally, we offer design implications for emotionally supporting users while mitigating the risks.
